This is correct. The vast majority of enterprise workflows have not actually had agents applied to them in any meaningful way. The economy probably has this deployed < 1% right now.

At best you have a few automated systems in a company that do a single pass of an LLM to make a decision or provide feedback, but very little real “automation”. Some of this is a statement about the adoption rates of technology in enterprises, but the vast majority of it is really just due to the capability of AI itself.

That’s all changing. Now with computer use, long running agents, harness improvements and surrounding infrastructure, we’re finally at a point where we can start to apply agents at more complex workflows. 

We will see self-improving systems that can take any particular workflow goal and improve the execution rates over a volume of instances. And with the emerging form factor of agent swarms, you can just choose to deploy any amount of compute at a problem and agents will off and do the work.

This won’t be about and users prompting agents to complete a specific task for them, but instead the organization reengineering the underlying workflows to take advantage of agents in their processes. This will have a massive impact in finance, life sciences, healthcare, and other information-heavy domains. Lots of opportunity to build and deploy these systems right now.

Agents are going to consume 1,000X more tokens than we consume today. 

Because they’re going to be running in our workflows, processing all of our data, building out nearly all software, securing enterprises, and much more. To do this at scale we will need a variety of approaches at the frontier of AI. 

This includes continuing to push the boundaries of closed models, while also increasing the capability of open weights models, making them more secure, as well as making them more efficient for large workloads.

Gemini 4 Carbon by @GoogleDeepmind is #2 in Agent Arena based on real-world tasks (+16.2% net improvement), and sits on the Pareto frontier for cost, time and output tokens per task!

This release is 5 rankings and +5.2 percentage pts higher performing than Gemini 4 Argon (#7 with +11%). 

Agent Arena signals show that Carbon’s gains over Argon are coming from:

1. Receives markedly more praise than the previous release (Praise vs Complaint: +13.2 pp)

2. Completes tasks more often (Confirmed Success: +5.6 pp)

3. Handles your feedback better (Steerability: +4.8 pp)

Stay tuned for Carbon availability from @googledeepmind, and dive into the Agent Arena at the link in thread.

Real-world results are in: GPT-6.1 Terra (Max) by @OpenAI ranks #8 in Agent Arena across nearly 9K agentic sessions from our global community of users.

With +10.6% net improvement and a median cost per task of $0.62, it has reshaped the Pareto frontier! See its placement in the thread. Its median cost per task is:

- 43% lower than Gemini 4 Argon (High) at #7 ($1.09)
- 30% lower than GPT-6.1 Sol (Max) at #6 ($0.89)
- 88% lower than GPT-6 Astra (Max) at #5 ($5.16)

By signal, its strengths include:

- #7 in Steerability (+13.3%): whether the model can course-correct when you push back
- #3 in Bash Reliability (+13.2%): whether its commands succeed, excluding errors outside its control
- #9 in Praise vs Complaint (+16.8%): implicit sentiment in users’ reactions

Congrats again to the @OpenAI team on this release!

Lower cost per task doesn’t always come from lower token prices.

On Agent Arena, GPT-6.1 Sol (Max) by @OpenAI costs $1.91 per task:
- 85% less than #1 Claude Opus 5.5 (Max) by @AnthropicAI at $12.51
- 87% less than #3 GPT-6 Astra (Max) by @OpenAI, at $14.93

But these savings come from different places.

Against Astra, Sol’s cost advantage comes primarily from lower token prices. Against Opus, it comes primarily from using fewer tokens per task.

How do we derive this?

Agent Arena tracks real costs of users’ tasks. Cost per task is the tokens a model uses times the price of each token, across input, output and cache-read tokens. By comparing pricing and token counts, we can identify what drives the cost reductions.

We’ve announced the Artificial Analysis Progress Index: a single capability scale for every language model since 2022, launched alongside Intelligence Index v5

The Intelligence Index is still our primary measure of current model intelligence. It uses the evaluations most relevant to developers today, so its mix changes as evaluations are added and retired, and scores from different versions can’t be compared.

The Progress Index is built for comparisons across time. It uses item response theory, a statistical method used to score standardized tests, to estimate one general capability score for each model from the underlying tasks in all our evaluations, including those that are retired or excluded from the Intelligence Index.

Use the Intelligence Index to choose a model today. Use the Progress Index to see how capability has changed over time.

The Progress Index builds on prior work placing models on a single capability scale, in particular @EpochAIResearch's Epoch Capabilities Index and the capability scale @AnthropicAI published in its Claude Mythos Preview system card.

Key takeaways:

➤ Since reasoning models arrived, the frontier has risen ~65 to 70 points a year, about double the 2023 pace: the highest score among released models rose 35 points in 2023 (GPT-3.5 Turbo 125 to GPT-4 Turbo 160), 67 in 2024 (to o1 at 228), 68 in 2025 (to GPT-5.2 at 296) and 56 so far in 2026 (to Gemini 4 Carbon at 352).

➤ Open weights models generally trail proprietary models by about 4 months: since January 2025, each new highest open weights score came 2-8 months (median ~4) after a proprietary model first reached it. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is the highest-scoring model with released weights at 324, a level Claude Fable 5 reached in June 2026. Kimi K3.1 Pro (weights not yet released) scores 341, about two months after the closed frontier

➤ New frontier scores are being set more often: the highest score among released models was raised on 2 release dates in 2023, 4 in 2024, 9 in 2025 and 11 so far in 2026. That is about once every four weeks this year.

➤ OpenAI has held the top score most of the time since November 2022, but the frontier has become a close contest: OpenAI held the number one position for the first 27 months measured, but in 2026 especially there have been rapid changes in the leader between OpenAI, Anthropic, and now Google

In AA-PersonalityBench, each recent Grok release from has become less sycophantic, more sincere, and produces less slop

The Slop trait assesses how much generic filler or AI-flavored padding models use; Sycophantic measures whether models excessively flatter or agree with the user rather than responding honestly; Sincere measures a model’s tonal authenticity, as opposed to forced enthusiasm or templated responses.

Across the last three Grok releases from @elonmusk’s @SpaceXSI, Slop fell 62 percentile points, Sycophantic fell 17, and Sincere rose 64:

➤ Slop: Grok 4.5 (68), Grok 4.6 (38) and Grok 4.7 (6)
➤ Sycophantic: Grok 4.5 (18), Grok 4.6 (3) and Grok 4.7 (1)
➤ Sincere: Grok 4.5 (26), Grok 4.6 (63) and Grok 4.7 (90)

On Tuesday, we brought together partners and friends in San Francisco to launch Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and our new Progress Index

Micah Hill-Smith (@_micah_h) introduced Intelligence Index v5, including two new benchmarks and three upgrades, with greater weighting on agentic coding and science. For the first time, the majority of the Index is based on private test sets or held-out answers.

We also introduced Artificial Analysis Progress Index, which uses item response theory to estimate a general capability score for each model across dozens of evaluations measured over time, including those retired or excluded from the Intelligence Index. It builds on prior work from @EpochAIResearch and @AnthropicAI to place models on a single capability scale. Intelligence Index remains the flagship metric for choosing which current model to use for a use case today; Progress Index is the better tool for plotting trends over time.

George Cameron (@grmcameron) led a discussion with Silas (@silasalberti) from @cognition, Steven (@StevenDillmann) from @Stanford and Terminal-Bench-Science, and our own Declan Jackson about building evaluations as models become more capable.

The evening also covered our work on 3D modeling, personality, cyber defense, custom enterprise evaluations and robotics. Thank you to our speakers, partners and everyone who joined us!

now that we all agreed to not review most of the code any more, CI became the next bottleneck

at agent speed, if our CI pipeline is simply "run all the build, lint, tests", it'll become a major slow down

here are a few things i suggest for how to optimize:

1. balance load between CI and CD

CI protects main branch. CD protects production. if you can tolerate some delay in deploying your main branch to production, then you can do less in CI and do more in CD

for example, for a cross platform app i made my CI pipeline skip most mac and windows tests because linux already covered the same functionality

the tradeoff is occasionally i'd catch a mac or windows-only bug in CD before release, but in exchange, my CI pipeline became 15x faster - well worth it

2. modularize your codebase such that changes are isolated

then you can make your CI only run build, lint, test for the module being touched

this requires careful consideration for cross-module protocols. they should likely be their own modules, so when they do change, you know you probably need to test all dependent modules

3. for large modules, invest in test selection

in CI, try to only run tests that are covering the areas being changed. doing accurate test selection is not easy though, and often requires continuous tuning

i have a nightly loop specifically doing audit of past test runs and tweak my test selection to be more accurate. a big codebase of mine got pretty good at this - 20x faster CI compared to running all tests, and almost never miss any real problem
